issues.legal_issue: The general jurisdiction to decide questions concerning execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree operates subject to the special restriction on recognising uncertified payments or adjustments.
material_facts: The dispute arose in proceedings to execute a decree.

The general provision gives the executing court jurisdiction over questions relating to execution, discharge, or satisfaction, while the specific provision bars recognition of an uncertified payment or adjustment.
Both provisions form part of the same statutory scheme governing execution of decrees.
issues.conclusion: The provisions are reconcilable: the general jurisdiction applies subject to the special restriction, and an uncertified adjustment cannot be recognised by the executing court.
issues.legal_principle: The court must read a statute as a whole and harmonise provisions where possible, avoiding an interpretation that makes either provision otiose. It relied on Canada Sugar Refining Co. v. R. (1898) AC 735; M. Pentiah v. Veeramallappa Muddala, AIR 1961 SC 1107; Gammon India Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1974 SC 960; Mysore State Road Transports Corporation v. Mirza Khasim Ali Beg, AIR 1977 SC 747; Vaddeboyina Tulsamme v. Vaddeboyina Sesha Reddi, AIR 1977 SC 1944; Punjab Beverages Pvt. Ltd. v. Suresh Chand, AIR 1978 SC 995; Commissioner of Income-tax v. National Taj Traders, AIR 1980 SC 485; Calcutta Gas Co. (Proprietary) Ltd. v. State of West Bengal, AIR 1962 SC 1044; and J.K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills v. State of U.P., AIR 1961 SC 1170. Applying the principle generalia specialibus non derogant, the general power under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure is subject to Order XXI Rule 2, including sub-rule (3), which governs payments and adjustments.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A court is considering the enforcement of a decree.
predicates.general_execution_question: The matter concerns a question about execution, discharge, or satisfaction of the decree.
predicates.special_adjustment_recording_rule_applie: A specific rule governs whether a payment or adjustment of the decree may be recognised.

issues.definition: When enforcement proceedings raise a general question about a decree and a specific rule governs the claimed adjustment, the general power operates subject to that specific rule.

issues.legal_issue: Delivery of possession in claimed satisfaction of an eviction decree is an adjustment that the executing court cannot recognise unless it has been certified or recorded as required.
material_facts: The decree required the occupant to vacate and deliver possession by a specified date.
The occupant objected to execution, claiming that he had delivered possession to the decree-holder’s attorney and had then been allowed to remain under a licence.
The claimed delivery and subsequent arrangement had not been certified or recorded by the executing court.
The executing court treated the decree as satisfied to the extent of delivery, and the High Court upheld that decision.
issues.conclusion: The claimed delivery of possession amounted to an adjustment of the eviction decree and, because it was not certified or recorded, could not be recognised; the decree remained executable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 47 and Order XXI Rule 2(1)–(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an adjustment that extinguishes a decree wholly or partly must be certified or recorded, and an uncertified adjustment cannot be recognised by the executing court. The court relied on Moti Lal Bankers v. Mohd. Hassan Khan, AIR 1968 SC 1087, and also noted the consistent approach in P. Narsaiah v. P. Rajoo Reddy, AIR 1989 AP 164; Bhabani Dasya v. Tulsi Ram Keot, AIR 1990 Guwahati 90; Rajeev Khandelwal v. Arun Pannalal, AIR 1987 MP 262; Krishna Gobind Patil v. Moolchand, AIR 1941 Bombay 302; Sham Lal Chatterjee v. Hazarimal Babu; and Biroo Gorain v. Musstt. Jaimurat Koer.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and eviction_decree_case and possession_claimed_as_satisfaction and adjustment_not_certified_or_recorded

predicates.execution_proceeding: A court is considering the enforcement of a decree.
predicates.eviction_decree_case: The decree requires an occupant to vacate premises and deliver possession.
predicates.possession_claimed_as_satisfaction: The judgment-debtor claims to have delivered possession in satisfaction of the decree.
predicates.adjustment_not_certified_or_recorded: The claimed delivery or related adjustment has not been certified or recorded by the executing court.

issues.definition: If, in an eviction-decree execution, the judgment-debtor relies on unrecorded delivery of possession as satisfaction, the court cannot recognise that adjustment and the decree remains executable.

issues.legal_issue: A post-decree licence to remain in premises does not extinguish or supersede an eviction decree where the parties did not create a fresh lease or intend to give up the rights under the decree.
material_facts: The occupant claimed that the decree-holder’s attorney allowed him to remain in the premises as a licensee after the alleged delivery of possession.
The occupant described the arrangement as a licence and claimed to pay a licence fee, rather than asserting that a fresh lease had been created.
The court held that the decree-holder’s rights under the eviction decree were preserved and that the alleged licence was intended only to permit temporary continued occupation.
issues.conclusion: The alleged licence did not destroy or supersede the eviction decree, which remained enforceable.
issues.legal_principle: Whether parties intended to surrender rights under a decree is decisive. A licence, involving permissive occupation rather than an interest in the property or a right to exclusive possession, does not by itself replace an eviction decree; a fresh lease could do so if that was the parties’ intention. The court relied on Konchada Ramamurty Subudhi v. Gopinath Naik, AIR 1968 SC 919; Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapur, AIR 1959 SC 1262; Smt. Kalloo v. Dhakadevi, AIR 1982 SC 813; and the stated test in Booker v. Palmer, (1942) 2 All ER 674.

rule.if: eviction_decree_case and post_decree_permission_to_remain and permission_was_a_licence and no_fresh_lease_created

predicates.eviction_decree_case: The decree requires an occupant to vacate premises and deliver possession.
predicates.post_decree_permission_to_remain: After the decree, the decree-holder or an authorised person permits the occupant to remain in the premises.
predicates.permission_was_a_licence: The permission is a licence allowing occupation rather than a transfer of an interest in the premises with exclusive possession.
predicates.no_fresh_lease_created: The parties did not create a fresh lease replacing the earlier relationship.

issues.definition: When an occupant subject to an eviction decree is later permitted to stay only as a licensee and no fresh lease is created, the decree remains enforceable.
